sentences.text: The genus Valdosaurus contains only one valid species, V. canaliculatus, which was originally based on femurs belonging to a young individual.
While the type material represents a juvenile, an adult of this medium-sized euornithopod would have possessed femurs reaching half a meter in length.
In life, the newly described specimen would have measured around 4 to 5 meters in length.
Although the type specimens were small, reaching only 10 kilograms in mass, larger individuals like the Compton Bay find may have weighed as much as 400 kilograms.
The tail vertebrae feature backswept neural spines that overhang more than one following vertebra, a trait distinct from other ornithischians.
Unlike other dryosaurids, Valdosaurus canaliculatus possesses an open obturator notch on the pubis bone.
Reverend William Darwin Fox collected two small femurs near Cowleaze Chine on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight during the 19th century.
In 1889, Richard Lydekker initially assigned these remains to Camptosaurus valdensis based on a partial lower jaw and other bones.
Peter Galton later concluded they did not belong to Camptosaurus and named them Dryosaurus canaliculatus in 1975.
Galton subsequently created the new genus Valdosaurus for this species in 1977.
Galton and Philippe Taquet described a second species, V. nigeriensis, from rocks in Niger in 1982.
However, in 2009, Galton concluded that fossils from outside England could not be reliably assigned to Valdosaurus and reclassified V. nigeriensis as Elrhazosaurus.
Nick Chase discovered a new Valdosaurus specimen in Compton Bay on the Isle of Wight in 2012, with the exact location withheld to prevent theft.
Sedimentological data suggests the depositional environment of the Wessex Formation was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits.
Burned plant and insect material and fusain suggest that the environment experienced frequent wildfires.
Valdosaurus is generally classified as a member of the family Dryosauridae.
Peter Galton originally assigned Valdosaurus to the paraphyletic family Hypsilophodontidae.
The genus belongs to the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
Valdosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately between 130 and 125 million years ago in the Barremian stage.
The dinosaur lived in what is now Europe, with fossils found on the Isle of Wight and other parts of England.
Some sources indicate Valdosaurus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Aptian stages, between 154.8 and 119.57 million years ago.
It is debated whether many English specimens, including cranial elements and teeth, truly belong to Valdosaurus.
The presence of Valdosaurus in Spain remains questionable.
